title: Retail COO on promo stockouts (medium, middle)
transcript:
Interviewer: Did you have any trouble finding the room this morning?
COO: None at all. The reception staff pointed me over, and the signs were pretty clear once I was on the right floor.
Interviewer: Has the company changed its branding recently?
COO: We refreshed the logo two summers ago. It was a modest change, mostly the colours, and the printed stationery took longer to get replaced than anyone expected.
Interviewer: Sorry, could you repeat that last part? I missed the end of it.
COO: Of course. It was a long answer, so don't worry if it rambled a little, I do that sometimes.
Interviewer: It's raining quite hard outside now, isn't it?
COO: It has been since early this morning. I got a bit wet on the walk over, but my coat is drying on the hook by the door.
Interviewer: Is the commute a problem for you?
COO: It's the worst part of my day. The trains are crowded and the delays are constant, and I seriously considered moving closer last year.
Interviewer: I'll move on to the next topic, if that works for you.
COO: Go ahead. I'm happy to follow wherever you want to take it, so just steer the conversation as you see fit.
Interviewer: What do people do for lunch?
COO: A mix of the canteen and the small cafe across the road. The cafe does a very good soup, and some people have their own table there on Fridays.
Interviewer: What do you do when you're not working?
COO: I play in a small amateur orchestra, which takes up most evenings. We have a concert coming up in a few weeks, and I'm still practising the hardest passage.
Interviewer: Walk me through why shelves go empty on your promoted items.
COO: Honestly, the promo calendar is built by marketing in January and replenishment only sees it two weeks before launch. By then the supplier lead time is already longer than the notice we have.
Interviewer: So who owns the gap?
COO: Nobody. Planning thinks marketing owns it, marketing thinks supply chain owns it. We lost roughly 4 percent of promo revenue last year to stockouts and nobody was accountable for that number.
Interviewer: What do the store managers do?
COO: They keep a private spreadsheet of what usually sells out and they over-order by instinct. It works for the experienced ones. The new managers just get burned.
Interviewer: Anything working well?
COO: Our weekly cross-functional call is actually good, people turn up. It just happens after the decisions are made.
Interviewer: Let me know if I start running over the time we agreed.
COO: We have until the top of the hour, so we're fine. After that I do have another commitment, but it's a short walk.
Interviewer: Is it alright if we take a short break soon?
COO: Sure, whenever suits you. I'm happy to carry on for a while longer if you want to get through a few more questions.
Interviewer: How is the IT equipment generally?
COO: Laptops get replaced every four years or so. The latest batch arrived in the autumn and people were pleased with the screens, though the chargers are a different story.
Interviewer: Do you use the intranet much?
COO: As little as possible. The search is useless, and I always end up asking a colleague where something is instead.
Interviewer: Do you have any teams based elsewhere?
COO: A small team in Lisbon handles our invoicing. I've only met them twice, but they sent a lovely card when we hit one of our anniversaries last year.
Interviewer: Has the office changed much recently?
COO: We moved floors a couple of years ago to make room for a new team. The new layout is brighter, though the meeting rooms are still in short supply on Tuesdays.
Interviewer: Is there anything people complain about that I should know of?
COO: Parking, mostly. It's been tight ever since the car park was resurfaced and the number of bays went down by a handful, and people get quite passionate about it.
Interviewer: Let me just make sure I've understood you correctly.
COO: Please do. It's better to check now than to find out later that we were each thinking about something slightly different.
Interviewer: What's the culture like day to day?
COO: Friendly, I'd say. We have a lunch-and-learn series on the first Thursday of every month, and attendance is surprisingly good considering it's over lunchtime.

COO: The roof terrace, if the weather holds. It was added two years ago and is the best spot in the building, though it closes the moment it gets properly cold.

COO: We have a quiz night every December, with teams drawn from different floors. The reception team won it three years in a row, and nobody has quite forgiven them.

COO: Just over nine years now. I started in a different role and moved across when the department was reorganised, which seems like a very long time ago.
Interviewer: I know it's a busy week, so I really appreciate you making the time.
COO: No problem at all. I moved a meeting to make room, and honestly it's a nice break from my desk.
Interviewer: Does the company run any training programmes?
COO: There's an induction week for new starters with a tour of all the sites. It's popular, although I think people mainly enjoy the free lunch on the last day.
Interviewer: Would you like me to send you a summary of what we discussed afterwards?
COO: That would be good, yes. Just send it to my work address, and I'll look it over when I have a quiet moment.
Interviewer: It's raining quite hard outside now, isn't it?
COO: It has been since early this morning. I got a bit wet on the walk over, but my coat is drying on the hook by the door.
Interviewer: I'll move on to the next topic, if that works for you.
COO: Go ahead. I'm happy to follow wherever you want to take it, so just steer the conversation as you see fit.

COO: Pretty much, yes. It's a running joke in the building, and half the people on this floor keep a small fan at their desk.
Interviewer: What do you make of the coffee here?
COO: Terrible, if I'm honest. It's the thing I complain about most, and I've started bringing my own flask in.

COO: Parking, mostly. It's been tight ever since the car park was resurfaced and the number of bays went down by a handful, and people get quite passionate about it.

transcript:
Interviewer: What do you think of the Monday all-staff emails?
COO: A bit much, honestly. They're far too long and I tend to skim them over a coffee and forget everything by lunchtime.
Interviewer: Thanks, that's really helpful to hear.
COO: Happy to help. Let me know if any of it needs more detail, and I can think about it and get back to you.
Interviewer: Is the building leased or owned?
COO: Leased. The lease was renewed for another five years last winter, and there was a short debate about whether to move, but in the end everyone was happy to stay.
Interviewer: I'll move on to the next topic, if that works for you.
COO: Go ahead. I'm happy to follow wherever you want to take it, so just steer the conversation as you see fit.
Interviewer: What's the culture like day to day?
COO: Friendly, I'd say. We have a lunch-and-learn series on the first Thursday of every month, and attendance is surprisingly good considering it's over lunchtime.
Interviewer: Does the company run any training programmes?
COO: There's an induction week for new starters with a tour of all the sites. It's popular, although I think people mainly enjoy the free lunch on the last day.
Interviewer: Is it alright if we take a short break soon?
COO: Sure, whenever suits you. I'm happy to carry on for a while longer if you want to get through a few more questions.
Interviewer: Are there any questions you'd like to ask me before we continue?
COO: Not right now, though I might have one or two at the end once I've had a chance to think about the whole conversation.
Interviewer: I know it's a busy week, so I really appreciate you making the time.
COO: No problem at all. I moved a meeting to make room, and honestly it's a nice break from my desk.
Interviewer: Does the company have a sustainability policy?
COO: We have a modest one. There's a recycling scheme on each floor, and last year we switched to a green electricity supplier, which was announced at an all-hands meeting.
Interviewer: How's the wifi in the meeting rooms?
COO: Hopeless, to be frank. It cuts out in the middle of calls, and I've given up trying to share my screen on the second floor.
Interviewer: Who else should I be talking to while I'm here?
COO: You could try the new finance lead, who joined in the spring. She's settled in quickly and has been a great addition, but I couldn't tell you much about her area.
Interviewer: I'll keep this fairly informal, so just say if something isn't clear.
COO: That sounds good to me. I tend to answer more naturally when it feels like a conversation rather than a formal interview.
Interviewer: How are the facilities?
COO: The canteen introduced a vegetarian day on Wednesdays, which went down better than expected. The coffee machine on the third floor still breaks every few weeks, though.
Interviewer: Could I ask you to speak up a little? The recorder is across the table.
COO: Certainly. I tend to trail off at the end of sentences, so do stop me if I become hard to hear on the recording.
Interviewer: Sorry, I lost my place in my notes for a moment.
COO: No worries at all, I do exactly that in my own meetings. Take as long as you need to find it again.
Interviewer: How do you find the new office layout?
COO: Honestly, a bit grim. The lighting on the fourth floor gives me a headache and I think most people would say the same if you asked them.
Interviewer: How's the canteen these days?
COO: Overpriced, I'd say. The food is fine but a sandwich costs more than it does across the road, and I don't think that's right.
Interviewer: Does the company do much outside the core business?
COO: We sponsor a local charity run every autumn. About forty colleagues take part, and it's become a bit of a tradition, with a small prize for the best fancy dress.
Interviewer: Tell me a little about the wider organisation.
COO: We're a few hundred people spread over three sites. The head office is the largest, and the other two are mostly small teams who've been with us for years.
Interviewer: Before we go on, are you happy for me to keep recording?
COO: Yes, that's fine, go ahead. I've done a few of these before, so I know roughly how it goes.
Interviewer: Sorry, could you repeat that last part? I missed the end of it.
COO: Of course. It was a long answer, so don't worry if it rambled a little, I do that sometimes.
Interviewer: Is it all right if I come back to that point a bit later?
COO: Of course, that's fine. Just remind me if I forget, because I do tend to lose track when the conversation moves on.
Interviewer: Just give me a second to check my notes.
COO: Take your time. I'm in no rush, and I've blocked out the whole morning for this anyway.
Interviewer: Any traditions I should know about?
COO: We have a quiz night every December, with teams drawn from different floors. The reception team won it three years in a row, and nobody has quite forgiven them.
Interviewer: Let me know if I start running over the time we agreed.
COO: We have until the top of the hour, so we're fine. After that I do have another commitment, but it's a short walk.
Interviewer: How do you usually spend the summer break?
COO: Usually a week by the coast with the family. Last year the weather was dreadful, but the children didn't mind, and we spent most of the time in the arcade.
Interviewer: How long have you been with the company?
COO: Just over nine years now. I started in a different role and moved across when the department was reorganised, which seems like a very long time ago.
Interviewer: Walk me through why shelves go empty on your promoted items.
COO: Honestly, the promo calendar is built by marketing in January and replenishment only sees it two weeks before launch. By then the supplier lead time is already longer than the notice we have.
Interviewer: So who owns the gap?
COO: Nobody. Planning thinks marketing owns it, marketing thinks supply chain owns it. We lost roughly 4 percent of promo revenue last year to stockouts and nobody was accountable for that number.
Interviewer: What do the store managers do?
COO: They keep a private spreadsheet of what usually sells out and they over-order by instinct. It works for the experienced ones. The new managers just get burned.
Interviewer: Anything working well?
COO: Our weekly cross-functional call is actually good, people turn up. It just happens after the decisions are made.
Interviewer: I'll try not to keep you much longer than planned.
COO: No rush from my side. I'd much rather we cover things properly than cut the conversation short because of the clock.
Interviewer: Was there a company event this year?
COO: Yes, the annual offsite was in the countryside. The weather was lovely, and the walk on the second morning turned out to be the part everybody remembered afterwards.
Interviewer: Has the office changed much recently?
COO: We moved floors a couple of years ago to make room for a new team. The new layout is brighter, though the meeting rooms are still in short supply on Tuesdays.
Interviewer: How has your week been so far?
COO: Busy, but nothing out of the ordinary. Monday was the worst of it, and things have been calmer since then.
Interviewer: Is there anything about the building you'd change?
COO: The lifts, definitely. They are always breaking down, and I have walked up seven flights more times than I'd like to admit.
Interviewer: Is there anything you'd like to show me on the tour?
COO: The roof terrace, if the weather holds. It was added two years ago and is the best spot in the building, though it closes the moment it gets properly cold.
Interviewer: Do you like the open-plan layout?
COO: Not really, no. It's noisy and there's nowhere to take a private call, so I end up in the stairwell more often than not.
Interviewer: Do you mind if I ask a couple of background questions first?
COO: Not at all, ask whatever you need. I'd rather you had the full picture than guessed at the parts I left out.
Interviewer: Is this still a good time, or are you expecting a call?
COO: It's fine, I've put my phone on silent. If anything urgent comes up my assistant knows where to find me.
Interviewer: How do you keep in touch with people on other sites?
COO: A monthly video call, mostly. It's more social than anything, with a rotating host who picks a theme, and last month's was baking, which went about as well as you'd imagine.
Interviewer: Is there anything people complain about that I should know of?
COO: Parking, mostly. It's been tight ever since the car park was resurfaced and the number of bays went down by a handful, and people get quite passionate about it.
Interviewer: Could you spell that name for my notes, please?
COO: Sure, it's the usual spelling, nothing unusual. I'll write it down for you if that's easier than saying it out loud.
Interviewer: Do you have any teams based elsewhere?
COO: A small team in Lisbon handles our invoicing. I've only met them twice, but they sent a lovely card when we hit one of our anniversaries last year.
Interviewer: Can you hear me properly? The speaker in this room sometimes crackles.
COO: I can hear you fine. It crackled a little at the start, but it seems to have settled down now.
Interviewer: How do you find the printers?
COO: Dreadful. They jam constantly, and nobody ever replaces the paper, so I've more or less stopped printing anything at all.
Interviewer: Do you use the intranet much?
COO: As little as possible. The search is useless, and I always end up asking a colleague where something is instead.
Interviewer: Did you travel in this morning?
COO: I came by train, and for once it was on time. The carriage was full, but I managed to find a seat by the window.
Interviewer: What's the company known for in the local area?
COO: Mostly as a good employer. People tend to stay a long time, and we get a lot of speculative applications, which the recruitment team find both flattering and exhausting.
Interviewer: Do you get many visitors to the office?
COO: A fair number. We have a visitor badge system that was updated last year, and the lobby has a screen that shows the names of people who are expected that day.
Interviewer: Thanks for bearing with all the questions so far.
COO: That's what I'm here for. It's actually useful for me too, since it makes me say things out loud that I rarely get to.
Interviewer: Can I get you some water or a coffee before we continue?
COO: A coffee would be great, thank you. Just milk, no sugar, and there's no hurry at all.
Interviewer: Any thoughts on the new lanyards?
COO: Pointless, if you ask me. They keep getting caught on chairs, and I can't see who they were meant to help.
Interviewer: Is there much staff turnover on the administrative side?
COO: Not really, no. The reception team has been the same for years, and one of them is about to celebrate twenty years with the company, so there's a cake being planned.
Interviewer: Let me just make sure I've understood you correctly.
COO: Please do. It's better to check now than to find out later that we were each thinking about something slightly different.
Interviewer: What do people do for lunch?
COO: A mix of the canteen and the small cafe across the road. The cafe does a very good soup, and some people have their own table there on Fridays.
Interviewer: What do you do when you're not working?
COO: I play in a small amateur orchestra, which takes up most evenings. We have a concert coming up in a few weeks, and I'm still practising the hardest passage.
Interviewer: How do people usually communicate internally?
COO: We relaunched the intranet in January. People mostly use it for the canteen menu and the staff directory, and the newsletter goes out every other Friday.
Interviewer: Do you have a favourite part of the building?
COO: The old library on the second floor. They kept the shelves when the offices were redone, and it's the quietest room we have, so it's always the first to be booked.

COO: None at all. The reception staff pointed me over, and the signs were pretty clear once I was on the right floor.
Interviewer: Do you have any teams based elsewhere?
COO: A small team in Lisbon handles our invoicing. I've only met them twice, but they sent a lovely card when we hit one of our anniversaries last year.
Interviewer: What do people do for lunch?
COO: A mix of the canteen and the small cafe across the road. The cafe does a very good soup, and some people have their own table there on Fridays.

COO: We relaunched the intranet in January. People mostly use it for the canteen menu and the staff directory, and the newsletter goes out every other Friday.
Interviewer: Could I ask you to speak up a little? The recorder is across the table.
COO: Certainly. I tend to trail off at the end of sentences, so do stop me if I become hard to hear on the recording.
Interviewer: Is this still a good time, or are you expecting a call?
COO: It's fine, I've put my phone on silent. If anything urgent comes up my assistant knows where to find me.
Interviewer: Can I get you some water or a coffee before we continue?
COO: A coffee would be great, thank you. Just milk, no sugar, and there's no hurry at all.
Interviewer: Is it alright if we take a short break soon?
COO: Sure, whenever suits you. I'm happy to carry on for a while longer if you want to get through a few more questions.

COO: We sponsor a local charity run every autumn. About forty colleagues take part, and it's become a bit of a tradition, with a small prize for the best fancy dress.

COO: Nobody. Planning thinks marketing owns it, marketing thinks supply chain owns it. We lost roughly 4 percent of promo revenue last year to stockouts and nobody was accountable for that number. Sorry, that came out more complicated than I meant.

COO: A fair number. We have a visitor badge system that was updated last year, and the lobby has a screen that shows the names of people who are expected that day.
Interviewer: Is there anything people complain about that I should know of?
COO: Parking, mostly. It's been tight ever since the car park was resurfaced and the number of bays went down by a handful, and people get quite passionate about it.
Interviewer: Is the building leased or owned?
COO: Leased. The lease was renewed for another five years last winter, and there was a short debate about whether to move, but in the end everyone was happy to stay.

Interviewer: Do you mind if I ask a couple of background questions first?
COO: Not at all, ask whatever you need. I'd rather you had the full picture than guessed at the parts I left out.

Interviewer: Thanks, that's really helpful to hear.

COO: We changed our booking tool last year, and the new one is much simpler. It cut the number of emails about hotels down considerably, which the assistants were pleased about.

Interviewer: How long have you been with the company?
COO: Just over nine years now. I started in a different role and moved across when the department was reorganised, which seems like a very long time ago.
Interviewer: Did you travel in this morning?
COO: I came by train, and for once it was on time. The carriage was full, but I managed to find a seat by the window.
Interviewer: What's the commute like for most people?
COO: Most people come by train or bike. We added secure bike storage last summer, and it filled up within a month, so there's now a waiting list for a space.
Interviewer: I'll try not to keep you much longer than planned.
COO: No rush from my side. I'd much rather we cover things properly than cut the conversation short because of the clock.
Interviewer: I'll keep this fairly informal, so just say if something isn't clear.
COO: That sounds good to me. I tend to answer more naturally when it feels like a conversation rather than a formal interview.
Interviewer: How are the facilities?
COO: The canteen introduced a vegetarian day on Wednesdays, which went down better than expected. The coffee machine on the third floor still breaks every few weeks, though.
Interviewer: Does the company have a sustainability policy?
COO: We have a modest one. There's a recycling scheme on each floor, and last year we switched to a green electricity supplier, which was announced at an all-hands meeting.
Interviewer: Who else should I be talking to while I'm here?
COO: You could try the new finance lead, who joined in the spring. She's settled in quickly and has been a great addition, but I couldn't tell you much about her area.
Interviewer: Could you spell that name for my notes, please?
COO: Sure, it's the usual spelling, nothing unusual. I'll write it down for you if that's easier than saying it out loud.
Interviewer: Let me just make sure I've understood you correctly.
COO: Please do. It's better to check now than to find out later that we were each thinking about something slightly different.
Interviewer: Anything working well?
COO: Our weekly cross-functional call is actually good, people turn up. It just happens after the decisions are made. Sorry, where was I?
Interviewer: How has your week been so far?
COO: Busy, but nothing out of the ordinary. Monday was the worst of it, and things have been calmer since then.
Interviewer: Is there much staff turnover on the administrative side?
COO: Not really, no. The reception team has been the same for years, and one of them is about to celebrate twenty years with the company, so there's a cake being planned.

COO: Dreadful. They jam constantly, and nobody ever replaces the paper, so I've more or less stopped printing anything at all.
Interviewer: How do you find the new office layout?
COO: Honestly, a bit grim. The lighting on the fourth floor gives me a headache and I think most people would say the same if you asked them.
Interviewer: Sorry, could you repeat that last part? I missed the end of it.
COO: Of course. It was a long answer, so don't worry if it rambled a little, I do that sometimes.
Interviewer: Before we go on, are you happy for me to keep recording?
COO: Yes, that's fine, go ahead. I've done a few of these before, so I know roughly how it goes.

COO: The lifts, definitely. They are always breaking down, and I have walked up seven flights more times than I'd like to admit.

Head of Surgery: A small team in Lisbon handles our invoicing. I've only met them twice, but they sent a lovely card when we hit one of our anniversaries last year.

Head of Surgery: It's the worst part of my day. The trains are crowded and the delays are constant, and I seriously considered moving closer last year.

Interviewer: Is it all right if I come back to that point a bit later?
Head of Surgery: Of course, that's fine. Just remind me if I forget, because I do tend to lose track when the conversation moves on.

Head of Surgery: Not at all, ask whatever you need. I'd rather you had the full picture than guessed at the parts I left out.
Interviewer: Who else should I be talking to while I'm here?
Head of Surgery: You could try the new finance lead, who joined in the spring. She's settled in quickly and has been a great addition, but I couldn't tell you much about her area.
Interviewer: Is there anything about the building you'd change?
Head of Surgery: The lifts, definitely. They are always breaking down, and I have walked up seven flights more times than I'd like to admit.
Interviewer: I'll try not to keep you much longer than planned.
Head of Surgery: No rush from my side. I'd much rather we cover things properly than cut the conversation short because of the clock.

Head of Surgery: Leased. The lease was renewed for another five years last winter, and there was a short debate about whether to move, but in the end everyone was happy to stay.
Interviewer: How is the IT equipment generally?
Head of Surgery: Laptops get replaced every four years or so. The latest batch arrived in the autumn and people were pleased with the screens, though the chargers are a different story.
Interviewer: What do you make of the coffee here?
Head of Surgery: Terrible, if I'm honest. It's the thing I complain about most, and I've started bringing my own flask in.
Interviewer: What do people do for lunch?
Head of Surgery: A mix of the canteen and the small cafe across the road. The cafe does a very good soup, and some people have their own table there on Fridays.

Head of Surgery: Pointless, if you ask me. They keep getting caught on chairs, and I can't see who they were meant to help.

Interviewer: What do you make of the coffee here?
VP Customer Success: Terrible, if I'm honest. It's the thing I complain about most, and I've started bringing my own flask in.
Interviewer: Just give me a second to check my notes.
VP Customer Success: Take your time. I'm in no rush, and I've blocked out the whole morning for this anyway.
Interviewer: Sorry, the call dropped on my end for a second there.
VP Customer Success: It was fine here, nothing missed. If it does drop again just give me a moment and I'll wait until you're back.
Interviewer: Is there much staff turnover on the administrative side?
VP Customer Success: Not really, no. The reception team has been the same for years, and one of them is about to celebrate twenty years with the company, so there's a cake being planned.
Interviewer: How do you keep in touch with people on other sites?
VP Customer Success: A monthly video call, mostly. It's more social than anything, with a rotating host who picks a theme, and last month's was baking, which went about as well as you'd imagine.
Interviewer: Does the company run any training programmes?
VP Customer Success: There's an induction week for new starters with a tour of all the sites. It's popular, although I think people mainly enjoy the free lunch on the last day.
Interviewer: I'll try not to keep you much longer than planned.
VP Customer Success: No rush from my side. I'd much rather we cover things properly than cut the conversation short because of the clock.
Interviewer: What's the company known for in the local area?
VP Customer Success: Mostly as a good employer. People tend to stay a long time, and we get a lot of speculative applications, which the recruitment team find both flattering and exhausting.
Interviewer: How's the canteen these days?
VP Customer Success: Overpriced, I'd say. The food is fine but a sandwich costs more than it does across the road, and I don't think that's right.
Interviewer: Any thoughts on the new lanyards?
VP Customer Success: Pointless, if you ask me. They keep getting caught on chairs, and I can't see who they were meant to help.
Interviewer: I'll move on to the next topic, if that works for you.
VP Customer Success: Go ahead. I'm happy to follow wherever you want to take it, so just steer the conversation as you see fit.
Interviewer: Do you mind if I ask a couple of background questions first?
VP Customer Success: Not at all, ask whatever you need. I'd rather you had the full picture than guessed at the parts I left out.
Interviewer: Do you get many visitors to the office?
VP Customer Success: A fair number. We have a visitor badge system that was updated last year, and the lobby has a screen that shows the names of people who are expected that day.
Interviewer: Is there anything about the building you'd change?
VP Customer Success: The lifts, definitely. They are always breaking down, and I have walked up seven flights more times than I'd like to admit.
Interviewer: Do you use the intranet much?
VP Customer Success: As little as possible. The search is useless, and I always end up asking a colleague where something is instead.
Interviewer: How do you find the printers?
VP Customer Success: Dreadful. They jam constantly, and nobody ever replaces the paper, so I've more or less stopped printing anything at all.
Interviewer: Is the commute a problem for you?
VP Customer Success: It's the worst part of my day. The trains are crowded and the delays are constant, and I seriously considered moving closer last year.
Interviewer: Thanks for bearing with all the questions so far.
VP Customer Success: That's what I'm here for. It's actually useful for me too, since it makes me say things out loud that I rarely get to.
Interviewer: Has the company changed its branding recently?
VP Customer Success: We refreshed the logo two summers ago. It was a modest change, mostly the colours, and the printed stationery took longer to get replaced than anyone expected.
Interviewer: Is the heating always this warm in here?
VP Customer Success: Pretty much, yes. It's a running joke in the building, and half the people on this floor keep a small fan at their desk.
Interviewer: I know it's a busy week, so I really appreciate you making the time.
VP Customer Success: No problem at all. I moved a meeting to make room, and honestly it's a nice break from my desk.
Interviewer: It's raining quite hard outside now, isn't it?
VP Customer Success: It has been since early this morning. I got a bit wet on the walk over, but my coat is drying on the hook by the door.
Interviewer: What do you think of the Monday all-staff emails?
VP Customer Success: A bit much, honestly. They're far too long and I tend to skim them over a coffee and forget everything by lunchtime.
Interviewer: Any traditions I should know about?
VP Customer Success: We have a quiz night every December, with teams drawn from different floors. The reception team won it three years in a row, and nobody has quite forgiven them.
Interviewer: Are there any questions you'd like to ask me before we continue?
VP Customer Success: Not right now, though I might have one or two at the end once I've had a chance to think about the whole conversation.
Interviewer: Thanks, that's really helpful to hear.
VP Customer Success: Happy to help. Let me know if any of it needs more detail, and I can think about it and get back to you.
Interviewer: How long have you been with the company?
VP Customer Success: Just over nine years now. I started in a different role and moved across when the department was reorganised, which seems like a very long time ago.
Interviewer: How do you usually spend the summer break?
VP Customer Success: Usually a week by the coast with the family. Last year the weather was dreadful, but the children didn't mind, and we spent most of the time in the arcade.
Interviewer: Tell me about the customers you lose.
VP Customer Success: Most churn happens in months four to six, right after onboarding ends. We hand the account to a pooled support team and the customer loses their named contact.
Interviewer: Is it a product problem?

Interviewer: What about pricing?
VP Customer Success: Everyone assumes it's price, including our CEO. The data does not support it. Discounted customers churn at the same rate as full price ones.
Interviewer: What would you change first?
VP Customer Success: Keep the onboarding owner on the account until month nine. It would cost two more hires and I can't get the budget approved.
Interviewer: Can I get you some water or a coffee before we continue?
VP Customer Success: A coffee would be great, thank you. Just milk, no sugar, and there's no hurry at all.
Interviewer: Who else should I be talking to while I'm here?
VP Customer Success: You could try the new finance lead, who joined in the spring. She's settled in quickly and has been a great addition, but I couldn't tell you much about her area.
Interviewer: Let me know if I start running over the time we agreed.
VP Customer Success: We have until the top of the hour, so we're fine. After that I do have another commitment, but it's a short walk.
Interviewer: How is the IT equipment generally?
VP Customer Success: Laptops get replaced every four years or so. The latest batch arrived in the autumn and people were pleased with the screens, though the chargers are a different story.
Interviewer: Do you have any teams based elsewhere?
VP Customer Success: A small team in Lisbon handles our invoicing. I've only met them twice, but they sent a lovely card when we hit one of our anniversaries last year.
Interviewer: Was there a company event this year?
VP Customer Success: Yes, the annual offsite was in the countryside. The weather was lovely, and the walk on the second morning turned out to be the part everybody remembered afterwards.
Interviewer: Would you like me to send you a summary of what we discussed afterwards?
VP Customer Success: That would be good, yes. Just send it to my work address, and I'll look it over when I have a quiet moment.
Interviewer: What's the culture like day to day?
VP Customer Success: Friendly, I'd say. We have a lunch-and-learn series on the first Thursday of every month, and attendance is surprisingly good considering it's over lunchtime.
Interviewer: Is there anything people complain about that I should know of?
VP Customer Success: Parking, mostly. It's been tight ever since the car park was resurfaced and the number of bays went down by a handful, and people get quite passionate about it.
Interviewer: Is this still a good time, or are you expecting a call?
VP Customer Success: It's fine, I've put my phone on silent. If anything urgent comes up my assistant knows where to find me.
Interviewer: Before we go on, are you happy for me to keep recording?
VP Customer Success: Yes, that's fine, go ahead. I've done a few of these before, so I know roughly how it goes.
Interviewer: How's the wifi in the meeting rooms?
VP Customer Success: Hopeless, to be frank. It cuts out in the middle of calls, and I've given up trying to share my screen on the second floor.
Interviewer: How do people usually communicate internally?
VP Customer Success: We relaunched the intranet in January. People mostly use it for the canteen menu and the staff directory, and the newsletter goes out every other Friday.
Interviewer: Has the office changed much recently?
VP Customer Success: We moved floors a couple of years ago to make room for a new team. The new layout is brighter, though the meeting rooms are still in short supply on Tuesdays.
Interviewer: How do you find the new office layout?
VP Customer Success: Honestly, a bit grim. The lighting on the fourth floor gives me a headache and I think most people would say the same if you asked them.
Interviewer: Did you travel in this morning?
VP Customer Success: I came by train, and for once it was on time. The carriage was full, but I managed to find a seat by the window.
Interviewer: Does the company do much outside the core business?
VP Customer Success: We sponsor a local charity run every autumn. About forty colleagues take part, and it's become a bit of a tradition, with a small prize for the best fancy dress.
Interviewer: Is the building leased or owned?
VP Customer Success: Leased. The lease was renewed for another five years last winter, and there was a short debate about whether to move, but in the end everyone was happy to stay.
Interviewer: Is it alright if we take a short break soon?
VP Customer Success: Sure, whenever suits you. I'm happy to carry on for a while longer if you want to get through a few more questions.
Interviewer: Does the company have a sustainability policy?
VP Customer Success: We have a modest one. There's a recycling scheme on each floor, and last year we switched to a green electricity supplier, which was announced at an all-hands meeting.
Interviewer: Do you have a favourite part of the building?
VP Customer Success: The old library on the second floor. They kept the shelves when the offices were redone, and it's the quietest room we have, so it's always the first to be booked.
Interviewer: Is there anything you'd like to show me on the tour?
VP Customer Success: The roof terrace, if the weather holds. It was added two years ago and is the best spot in the building, though it closes the moment it gets properly cold.
Interviewer: I'll keep this fairly informal, so just say if something isn't clear.
VP Customer Success: That sounds good to me. I tend to answer more naturally when it feels like a conversation rather than a formal interview.
Interviewer: Can you hear me properly? The speaker in this room sometimes crackles.
VP Customer Success: I can hear you fine. It crackled a little at the start, but it seems to have settled down now.
Interviewer: Do you like the open-plan layout?
VP Customer Success: Not really, no. It's noisy and there's nowhere to take a private call, so I end up in the stairwell more often than not.
Interviewer: How has your week been so far?
VP Customer Success: Busy, but nothing out of the ordinary. Monday was the worst of it, and things have been calmer since then.
Interviewer: Tell me a little about the wider organisation.
VP Customer Success: We're a few hundred people spread over three sites. The head office is the largest, and the other two are mostly small teams who've been with us for years.
Interviewer: Sorry, could you repeat that last part? I missed the end of it.
VP Customer Success: Of course. It was a long answer, so don't worry if it rambled a little, I do that sometimes.

Chief Compliance Officer: Friendly, I'd say. We have a lunch-and-learn series on the first Thursday of every month, and attendance is surprisingly good considering it's over lunchtime.
Interviewer: How do you find the new office layout?
Chief Compliance Officer: Honestly, a bit grim. The lighting on the fourth floor gives me a headache and I think most people would say the same if you asked them.
Interviewer: Before we go on, are you happy for me to keep recording?
Chief Compliance Officer: Yes, that's fine, go ahead. I've done a few of these before, so I know roughly how it goes.

Chief Compliance Officer: We refreshed the logo two summers ago. It was a modest change, mostly the colours, and the printed stationery took longer to get replaced than anyone expected.

Chief Compliance Officer: No rush from my side. I'd much rather we cover things properly than cut the conversation short because of the clock.

Chief Compliance Officer: We sponsor a local charity run every autumn. About forty colleagues take part, and it's become a bit of a tradition, with a small prize for the best fancy dress.
Interviewer: How do you usually spend the summer break?
Chief Compliance Officer: Usually a week by the coast with the family. Last year the weather was dreadful, but the children didn't mind, and we spent most of the time in the arcade.
Interviewer: How do people usually communicate internally?
Chief Compliance Officer: We relaunched the intranet in January. People mostly use it for the canteen menu and the staff directory, and the newsletter goes out every other Friday.
Interviewer: Did you travel in this morning?
Chief Compliance Officer: I came by train, and for once it was on time. The carriage was full, but I managed to find a seat by the window.
Interviewer: How has your week been so far?
Chief Compliance Officer: Busy, but nothing out of the ordinary. Monday was the worst of it, and things have been calmer since then.
Interviewer: Do you have a favourite part of the building?
Chief Compliance Officer: The old library on the second floor. They kept the shelves when the offices were redone, and it's the quietest room we have, so it's always the first to be booked.
Interviewer: Has the office changed much recently?
Chief Compliance Officer: We moved floors a couple of years ago to make room for a new team. The new layout is brighter, though the meeting rooms are still in short supply on Tuesdays.
Interviewer: What do you think of the Monday all-staff emails?
Chief Compliance Officer: A bit much, honestly. They're far too long and I tend to skim them over a coffee and forget everything by lunchtime.
Interviewer: Just give me a second to check my notes.
Chief Compliance Officer: Take your time. I'm in no rush, and I've blocked out the whole morning for this anyway.
Interviewer: I'll keep this fairly informal, so just say if something isn't clear.
Chief Compliance Officer: That sounds good to me. I tend to answer more naturally when it feels like a conversation rather than a formal interview.

Interviewer: Is there anything about the building you'd change?
Chief Compliance Officer: The lifts, definitely. They are always breaking down, and I have walked up seven flights more times than I'd like to admit.
Interviewer: What about travel? Do people get out much?
Chief Compliance Officer: We changed our booking tool last year, and the new one is much simpler. It cut the number of emails about hotels down considerably, which the assistants were pleased about.
Interviewer: Do you like the open-plan layout?
Chief Compliance Officer: Not really, no. It's noisy and there's nowhere to take a private call, so I end up in the stairwell more often than not.
Interviewer: Do you get many visitors to the office?
Chief Compliance Officer: A fair number. We have a visitor badge system that was updated last year, and the lobby has a screen that shows the names of people who are expected that day.
Interviewer: I know it's a busy week, so I really appreciate you making the time.
Chief Compliance Officer: No problem at all. I moved a meeting to make room, and honestly it's a nice break from my desk.

Chief Compliance Officer: A coffee would be great, thank you. Just milk, no sugar, and there's no hurry at all.

Interviewer: Did you have any trouble finding the room this morning?
Chief Compliance Officer: None at all. The reception staff pointed me over, and the signs were pretty clear once I was on the right floor.
Interviewer: Is there anything you'd like to show me on the tour?
Chief Compliance Officer: The roof terrace, if the weather holds. It was added two years ago and is the best spot in the building, though it closes the moment it gets properly cold.
Interviewer: Does the company have a sustainability policy?
Chief Compliance Officer: We have a modest one. There's a recycling scheme on each floor, and last year we switched to a green electricity supplier, which was announced at an all-hands meeting.
Interviewer: Do you have any teams based elsewhere?
Chief Compliance Officer: A small team in Lisbon handles our invoicing. I've only met them twice, but they sent a lovely card when we hit one of our anniversaries last year.
Interviewer: How's the canteen these days?
Chief Compliance Officer: Overpriced, I'd say. The food is fine but a sandwich costs more than it does across the road, and I don't think that's right.
Interviewer: Thanks for bearing with all the questions so far.
Chief Compliance Officer: That's what I'm here for. It's actually useful for me too, since it makes me say things out loud that I rarely get to.
Interviewer: Is this still a good time, or are you expecting a call?
Chief Compliance Officer: It's fine, I've put my phone on silent. If anything urgent comes up my assistant knows where to find me.
Interviewer: Sorry, the call dropped on my end for a second there.
Chief Compliance Officer: It was fine here, nothing missed. If it does drop again just give me a moment and I'll wait until you're back.
Interviewer: Sorry, could you repeat that last part? I missed the end of it.
Chief Compliance Officer: Of course. It was a long answer, so don't worry if it rambled a little, I do that sometimes.
Interviewer: Sorry, I lost my place in my notes for a moment.
Chief Compliance Officer: No worries at all, I do exactly that in my own meetings. Take as long as you need to find it again.
Interviewer: Is the building leased or owned?
Chief Compliance Officer: Leased. The lease was renewed for another five years last winter, and there was a short debate about whether to move, but in the end everyone was happy to stay.
Interviewer: What was the company like when you joined?
Chief Compliance Officer: Smaller and a bit scruffier. We had about half the staff and shared desks in a cramped open room, but there was a lot of goodwill and everyone knew everyone.
Interviewer: Any thoughts on the new lanyards?
Chief Compliance Officer: Pointless, if you ask me. They keep getting caught on chairs, and I can't see who they were meant to help.
Interviewer: How do you keep in touch with people on other sites?
Chief Compliance Officer: A monthly video call, mostly. It's more social than anything, with a rotating host who picks a theme, and last month's was baking, which went about as well as you'd imagine.
Interviewer: Is there much staff turnover on the administrative side?
Chief Compliance Officer: Not really, no. The reception team has been the same for years, and one of them is about to celebrate twenty years with the company, so there's a cake being planned.
Interviewer: What's the commute like for most people?
Chief Compliance Officer: Most people come by train or bike. We added secure bike storage last summer, and it filled up within a month, so there's now a waiting list for a space.
Interviewer: Any traditions I should know about?
Chief Compliance Officer: We have a quiz night every December, with teams drawn from different floors. The reception team won it three years in a row, and nobody has quite forgiven them.
Interviewer: Is the heating always this warm in here?
Chief Compliance Officer: Pretty much, yes. It's a running joke in the building, and half the people on this floor keep a small fan at their desk.
Interviewer: Do you mind if I ask a couple of background questions first?
Chief Compliance Officer: Not at all, ask whatever you need. I'd rather you had the full picture than guessed at the parts I left out.
Interviewer: Tell me a little about the wider organisation.
Chief Compliance Officer: We're a few hundred people spread over three sites. The head office is the largest, and the other two are mostly small teams who've been with us for years.

Chief Compliance Officer: Not right now, though I might have one or two at the end once I've had a chance to think about the whole conversation.

Chief Compliance Officer: Sure, whenever suits you. I'm happy to carry on for a while longer if you want to get through a few more questions.
Interviewer: How's the wifi in the meeting rooms?
Chief Compliance Officer: Hopeless, to be frank. It cuts out in the middle of calls, and I've given up trying to share my screen on the second floor.
Interviewer: Could I ask you to speak up a little? The recorder is across the table.
Chief Compliance Officer: Certainly. I tend to trail off at the end of sentences, so do stop me if I become hard to hear on the recording.
Interviewer: Can you hear me properly? The speaker in this room sometimes crackles.
Chief Compliance Officer: I can hear you fine. It crackled a little at the start, but it seems to have settled down now.
Interviewer: Would you like me to send you a summary of what we discussed afterwards?
Chief Compliance Officer: That would be good, yes. Just send it to my work address, and I'll look it over when I have a quiet moment.
Interviewer: Let me just make sure I've understood you correctly.
Chief Compliance Officer: Please do. It's better to check now than to find out later that we were each thinking about something slightly different.
Interviewer: Could you spell that name for my notes, please?
Chief Compliance Officer: Sure, it's the usual spelling, nothing unusual. I'll write it down for you if that's easier than saying it out loud.
Interviewer: Does the company run any training programmes?
Chief Compliance Officer: There's an induction week for new starters with a tour of all the sites. It's popular, although I think people mainly enjoy the free lunch on the last day.
Interviewer: Is there anything people complain about that I should know of?
Chief Compliance Officer: Parking, mostly. It's been tight ever since the car park was resurfaced and the number of bays went down by a handful, and people get quite passionate about it.
Interviewer: What do you make of the coffee here?
Chief Compliance Officer: Terrible, if I'm honest. It's the thing I complain about most, and I've started bringing my own flask in.

Interviewer: Just give me a second to check my notes.
Chief Compliance Officer: Take your time. I'm in no rush, and I've blocked out the whole morning for this anyway.
Interviewer: Sorry, the call dropped on my end for a second there.
Chief Compliance Officer: It was fine here, nothing missed. If it does drop again just give me a moment and I'll wait until you're back.
Interviewer: What's the company known for in the local area?
Chief Compliance Officer: Mostly as a good employer. People tend to stay a long time, and we get a lot of speculative applications, which the recruitment team find both flattering and exhausting.
Interviewer: Does the company do much outside the core business?
Chief Compliance Officer: We sponsor a local charity run every autumn. About forty colleagues take part, and it's become a bit of a tradition, with a small prize for the best fancy dress.
Interviewer: Is there anything people complain about that I should know of?
Chief Compliance Officer: Parking, mostly. It's been tight ever since the car park was resurfaced and the number of bays went down by a handful, and people get quite passionate about it.
Interviewer: How are the facilities?
Chief Compliance Officer: The canteen introduced a vegetarian day on Wednesdays, which went down better than expected. The coffee machine on the third floor still breaks every few weeks, though.
Interviewer: I'll try not to keep you much longer than planned.
Chief Compliance Officer: No rush from my side. I'd much rather we cover things properly than cut the conversation short because of the clock.
Interviewer: Tell me a little about the wider organisation.
Chief Compliance Officer: We're a few hundred people spread over three sites. The head office is the largest, and the other two are mostly small teams who've been with us for years.
Interviewer: Does the team ever get together outside work?
Chief Compliance Officer: Every so often. There's a Friday drinks tradition that started during the lockdowns and has carried on, and it's usually the same dozen people who turn up.
Interviewer: I know it's a busy week, so I really appreciate you making the time.
Chief Compliance Officer: No problem at all. I moved a meeting to make room, and honestly it's a nice break from my desk.
Interviewer: How's the canteen these days?
Chief Compliance Officer: Overpriced, I'd say. The food is fine but a sandwich costs more than it does across the road, and I don't think that's right.
Interviewer: Is it all right if I come back to that point a bit later?
Chief Compliance Officer: Of course, that's fine. Just remind me if I forget, because I do tend to lose track when the conversation moves on.
Interviewer: Can you hear me properly? The speaker in this room sometimes crackles.
Chief Compliance Officer: I can hear you fine. It crackled a little at the start, but it seems to have settled down now.
Interviewer: What do people do for lunch?
Chief Compliance Officer: A mix of the canteen and the small cafe across the road. The cafe does a very good soup, and some people have their own table there on Fridays.
Interviewer: Thanks for bearing with all the questions so far.
Chief Compliance Officer: That's what I'm here for. It's actually useful for me too, since it makes me say things out loud that I rarely get to.
Interviewer: What do you make of the coffee here?
Chief Compliance Officer: Terrible, if I'm honest. It's the thing I complain about most, and I've started bringing my own flask in.
Interviewer: Is this still a good time, or are you expecting a call?
Chief Compliance Officer: It's fine, I've put my phone on silent. If anything urgent comes up my assistant knows where to find me.
Interviewer: What was the company like when you joined?
Chief Compliance Officer: Smaller and a bit scruffier. We had about half the staff and shared desks in a cramped open room, but there was a lot of goodwill and everyone knew everyone.
Interviewer: Is the commute a problem for you?
Chief Compliance Officer: It's the worst part of my day. The trains are crowded and the delays are constant, and I seriously considered moving closer last year.
Interviewer: Did you travel in this morning?
Chief Compliance Officer: I came by train, and for once it was on time. The carriage was full, but I managed to find a seat by the window.
Interviewer: Before we go on, are you happy for me to keep recording?
Chief Compliance Officer: Yes, that's fine, go ahead. I've done a few of these before, so I know roughly how it goes.
Interviewer: I'll keep this fairly informal, so just say if something isn't clear.
Chief Compliance Officer: That sounds good to me. I tend to answer more naturally when it feels like a conversation rather than a formal interview.
Interviewer: Is it alright if we take a short break soon?
Chief Compliance Officer: Sure, whenever suits you. I'm happy to carry on for a while longer if you want to get through a few more questions.
Interviewer: Has the office changed much recently?
Chief Compliance Officer: We moved floors a couple of years ago to make room for a new team. The new layout is brighter, though the meeting rooms are still in short supply on Tuesdays.
Interviewer: Do you get many visitors to the office?
Chief Compliance Officer: A fair number. We have a visitor badge system that was updated last year, and the lobby has a screen that shows the names of people who are expected that day.
Interviewer: Has the company changed its branding recently?
Chief Compliance Officer: We refreshed the logo two summers ago. It was a modest change, mostly the colours, and the printed stationery took longer to get replaced than anyone expected.
Interviewer: Was there a company event this year?
Chief Compliance Officer: Yes, the annual offsite was in the countryside. The weather was lovely, and the walk on the second morning turned out to be the part everybody remembered afterwards.
Interviewer: Sorry, could you repeat that last part? I missed the end of it.
Chief Compliance Officer: Of course. It was a long answer, so don't worry if it rambled a little, I do that sometimes.
Interviewer: How does a new product get through compliance?
Chief Compliance Officer: Formally in six weeks. In practice it's closer to fourteen because product teams submit incomplete files and we spend weeks chasing missing documents.
Interviewer: Why are files incomplete?
Chief Compliance Officer: The checklist lives in a PDF from 2019 that nobody has updated, so teams don't know what we actually require now.
Interviewer: Do you have enough people?
Chief Compliance Officer: Headcount is fine. What we lack is a triage step, so a trivial fee change waits in the same queue as a new lending product.
Interviewer: Does the business see compliance as a blocker?
Chief Compliance Officer: Yes, and frankly they have a point on timing, though not on substance.
Interviewer: Could I ask you to speak up a little? The recorder is across the table.
Chief Compliance Officer: Certainly. I tend to trail off at the end of sentences, so do stop me if I become hard to hear on the recording.
Interviewer: It's raining quite hard outside now, isn't it?
Chief Compliance Officer: It has been since early this morning. I got a bit wet on the walk over, but my coat is drying on the hook by the door.
Interviewer: What about travel? Do people get out much?
Chief Compliance Officer: We changed our booking tool last year, and the new one is much simpler. It cut the number of emails about hotels down considerably, which the assistants were pleased about.
Interviewer: Could you spell that name for my notes, please?
Chief Compliance Officer: Sure, it's the usual spelling, nothing unusual. I'll write it down for you if that's easier than saying it out loud.
Interviewer: Do you have any teams based elsewhere?
Chief Compliance Officer: A small team in Lisbon handles our invoicing. I've only met them twice, but they sent a lovely card when we hit one of our anniversaries last year.
Interviewer: What do you think of the Monday all-staff emails?
Chief Compliance Officer: A bit much, honestly. They're far too long and I tend to skim them over a coffee and forget everything by lunchtime.
Interviewer: How do people usually communicate internally?
Chief Compliance Officer: We relaunched the intranet in January. People mostly use it for the canteen menu and the staff directory, and the newsletter goes out every other Friday.
Interviewer: Who else should I be talking to while I'm here?
Chief Compliance Officer: You could try the new finance lead, who joined in the spring. She's settled in quickly and has been a great addition, but I couldn't tell you much about her area.
Interviewer: I'll move on to the next topic, if that works for you.
Chief Compliance Officer: Go ahead. I'm happy to follow wherever you want to take it, so just steer the conversation as you see fit.
Interviewer: What's the commute like for most people?
Chief Compliance Officer: Most people come by train or bike. We added secure bike storage last summer, and it filled up within a month, so there's now a waiting list for a space.
Interviewer: How's the wifi in the meeting rooms?
Chief Compliance Officer: Hopeless, to be frank. It cuts out in the middle of calls, and I've given up trying to share my screen on the second floor.
Interviewer: Can I get you some water or a coffee before we continue?
Chief Compliance Officer: A coffee would be great, thank you. Just milk, no sugar, and there's no hurry at all.
Interviewer: Did you have any trouble finding the room this morning?
Chief Compliance Officer: None at all. The reception staff pointed me over, and the signs were pretty clear once I was on the right floor.
Interviewer: How do you usually spend the summer break?
Chief Compliance Officer: Usually a week by the coast with the family. Last year the weather was dreadful, but the children didn't mind, and we spent most of the time in the arcade.
Interviewer: How has your week been so far?
Chief Compliance Officer: Busy, but nothing out of the ordinary. Monday was the worst of it, and things have been calmer since then.
Interviewer: Does the company have a sustainability policy?
Chief Compliance Officer: We have a modest one. There's a recycling scheme on each floor, and last year we switched to a green electricity supplier, which was announced at an all-hands meeting.
Interviewer: Do you mind if I ask a couple of background questions first?
Chief Compliance Officer: Not at all, ask whatever you need. I'd rather you had the full picture than guessed at the parts I left out.
Interviewer: Do you like the open-plan layout?
Chief Compliance Officer: Not really, no. It's noisy and there's nowhere to take a private call, so I end up in the stairwell more often than not.
Interviewer: Thanks, that's really helpful to hear.
Chief Compliance Officer: Happy to help. Let me know if any of it needs more detail, and I can think about it and get back to you.
Interviewer: Let me know if I start running over the time we agreed.
Chief Compliance Officer: We have until the top of the hour, so we're fine. After that I do have another commitment, but it's a short walk.
Interviewer: What's the culture like day to day?
Chief Compliance Officer: Friendly, I'd say. We have a lunch-and-learn series on the first Thursday of every month, and attendance is surprisingly good considering it's over lunchtime.
Interviewer: How do you find the printers?
Chief Compliance Officer: Dreadful. They jam constantly, and nobody ever replaces the paper, so I've more or less stopped printing anything at all.
Interviewer: How long have you been with the company?
Chief Compliance Officer: Just over nine years now. I started in a different role and moved across when the department was reorganised, which seems like a very long time ago.
Interviewer: Are there any questions you'd like to ask me before we continue?
Chief Compliance Officer: Not right now, though I might have one or two at the end once I've had a chance to think about the whole conversation.
Interviewer: Would you like me to send you a summary of what we discussed afterwards?
Chief Compliance Officer: That would be good, yes. Just send it to my work address, and I'll look it over when I have a quiet moment.
Interviewer: Any thoughts on the new lanyards?
Chief Compliance Officer: Pointless, if you ask me. They keep getting caught on chairs, and I can't see who they were meant to help.
Interviewer: Let me just make sure I've understood you correctly.
Chief Compliance Officer: Please do. It's better to check now than to find out later that we were each thinking about something slightly different.
Interviewer: Is there much staff turnover on the administrative side?
Chief Compliance Officer: Not really, no. The reception team has been the same for years, and one of them is about to celebrate twenty years with the company, so there's a cake being planned.

Interviewer: Tell me a little about the wider organisation.

Chief Compliance Officer: Pointless, if you ask me. They keep getting caught on chairs, and I can't see who they were meant to help.
Interviewer: Can you hear me properly? The speaker in this room sometimes crackles.
Chief Compliance Officer: I can hear you fine. It crackled a little at the start, but it seems to have settled down now.

Chief Compliance Officer: There's an induction week for new starters with a tour of all the sites. It's popular, although I think people mainly enjoy the free lunch on the last day.
Interviewer: Is there anything you'd like to show me on the tour?
Chief Compliance Officer: The roof terrace, if the weather holds. It was added two years ago and is the best spot in the building, though it closes the moment it gets properly cold.
Interviewer: How does a new product get through compliance?
Chief Compliance Officer: Formally in six weeks. In practice it's closer to fourteen because product teams submit incomplete files and we spend weeks chasing missing documents. Sorry, my phone just buzzed.
Interviewer: How do you keep in touch with people on other sites?
Chief Compliance Officer: A monthly video call, mostly. It's more social than anything, with a rotating host who picks a theme, and last month's was baking, which went about as well as you'd imagine.
Interviewer: Any traditions I should know about?
Chief Compliance Officer: We have a quiz night every December, with teams drawn from different floors. The reception team won it three years in a row, and nobody has quite forgiven them.
Interviewer: It's raining quite hard outside now, isn't it?
Chief Compliance Officer: It has been since early this morning. I got a bit wet on the walk over, but my coat is drying on the hook by the door.
Interviewer: Before we go on, are you happy for me to keep recording?
Chief Compliance Officer: Yes, that's fine, go ahead. I've done a few of these before, so I know roughly how it goes.
Interviewer: Would you like me to send you a summary of what we discussed afterwards?
Chief Compliance Officer: That would be good, yes. Just send it to my work address, and I'll look it over when I have a quiet moment.
Interviewer: How long have you been with the company?
Chief Compliance Officer: Just over nine years now. I started in a different role and moved across when the department was reorganised, which seems like a very long time ago.
Interviewer: Sorry, could you repeat that last part? I missed the end of it.
Chief Compliance Officer: Of course. It was a long answer, so don't worry if it rambled a little, I do that sometimes.

Chief Compliance Officer: We have a modest one. There's a recycling scheme on each floor, and last year we switched to a green electricity supplier, which was announced at an all-hands meeting.
Interviewer: What do you make of the coffee here?
Chief Compliance Officer: Terrible, if I'm honest. It's the thing I complain about most, and I've started bringing my own flask in.
Interviewer: Is it alright if we take a short break soon?
Chief Compliance Officer: Sure, whenever suits you. I'm happy to carry on for a while longer if you want to get through a few more questions.
Interviewer: What about travel? Do people get out much?
Chief Compliance Officer: We changed our booking tool last year, and the new one is much simpler. It cut the number of emails about hotels down considerably, which the assistants were pleased about.
Interviewer: Has the office changed much recently?
Chief Compliance Officer: We moved floors a couple of years ago to make room for a new team. The new layout is brighter, though the meeting rooms are still in short supply on Tuesdays.
Interviewer: Why are files incomplete?
Chief Compliance Officer: The checklist lives in a PDF from 2019 that nobody has updated, so teams don't know what we actually require now. Sorry, where was I?

Interviewer: How has your week been so far?

Interviewer: Is there much staff turnover on the administrative side?

Chief Compliance Officer: As little as possible. The search is useless, and I always end up asking a colleague where something is instead.
Interviewer: What was the company like when you joined?
Chief Compliance Officer: Smaller and a bit scruffier. We had about half the staff and shared desks in a cramped open room, but there was a lot of goodwill and everyone knew everyone.
Interviewer: Sorry, I lost my place in my notes for a moment.
Chief Compliance Officer: No worries at all, I do exactly that in my own meetings. Take as long as you need to find it again.
Interviewer: How are the facilities?
Chief Compliance Officer: The canteen introduced a vegetarian day on Wednesdays, which went down better than expected. The coffee machine on the third floor still breaks every few weeks, though.
Interviewer: Did you have any trouble finding the room this morning?
Chief Compliance Officer: None at all. The reception staff pointed me over, and the signs were pretty clear once I was on the right floor.
Interviewer: How do you usually spend the summer break?
Chief Compliance Officer: Usually a week by the coast with the family. Last year the weather was dreadful, but the children didn't mind, and we spent most of the time in the arcade.
Interviewer: Is it all right if I come back to that point a bit later?
Chief Compliance Officer: Of course, that's fine. Just remind me if I forget, because I do tend to lose track when the conversation moves on.
Interviewer: Do you have enough people?
Chief Compliance Officer: Headcount is fine. What we lack is a triage step, so a trivial fee change waits in the same queue as a new lending product.
Interviewer: I'll move on to the next topic, if that works for you.
Chief Compliance Officer: Go ahead. I'm happy to follow wherever you want to take it, so just steer the conversation as you see fit.
Interviewer: Do you have any teams based elsewhere?
Chief Compliance Officer: A small team in Lisbon handles our invoicing. I've only met them twice, but they sent a lovely card when we hit one of our anniversaries last year.
Interviewer: How is the IT equipment generally?
Chief Compliance Officer: Laptops get replaced every four years or so. The latest batch arrived in the autumn and people were pleased with the screens, though the chargers are a different story.
Interviewer: Has the company changed its branding recently?
Chief Compliance Officer: We refreshed the logo two summers ago. It was a modest change, mostly the colours, and the printed stationery took longer to get replaced than anyone expected.
Interviewer: Is the commute a problem for you?
Chief Compliance Officer: It's the worst part of my day. The trains are crowded and the delays are constant, and I seriously considered moving closer last year.
Interviewer: I'll keep this fairly informal, so just say if something isn't clear.
Chief Compliance Officer: That sounds good to me. I tend to answer more naturally when it feels like a conversation rather than a formal interview.
Interviewer: What's the company known for in the local area?
Chief Compliance Officer: Mostly as a good employer. People tend to stay a long time, and we get a lot of speculative applications, which the recruitment team find both flattering and exhausting.
Interviewer: Just give me a second to check my notes.
Chief Compliance Officer: Take your time. I'm in no rush, and I've blocked out the whole morning for this anyway.
Interviewer: Do you mind if I ask a couple of background questions first?
Chief Compliance Officer: Not at all, ask whatever you need. I'd rather you had the full picture than guessed at the parts I left out.
Interviewer: Do you like the open-plan layout?
Chief Compliance Officer: Not really, no. It's noisy and there's nowhere to take a private call, so I end up in the stairwell more often than not.
Interviewer: Was there a company event this year?
Chief Compliance Officer: Yes, the annual offsite was in the countryside. The weather was lovely, and the walk on the second morning turned out to be the part everybody remembered afterwards.
Interviewer: Are there any questions you'd like to ask me before we continue?
Chief Compliance Officer: Not right now, though I might have one or two at the end once I've had a chance to think about the whole conversation.
Interviewer: Does the business see compliance as a blocker?
Chief Compliance Officer: Yes, and frankly they have a point on timing, though not on substance.
Interviewer: Thanks, that's really helpful to hear.
Chief Compliance Officer: Happy to help. Let me know if any of it needs more detail, and I can think about it and get back to you.
Interviewer: What's the culture like day to day?
Chief Compliance Officer: Friendly, I'd say. We have a lunch-and-learn series on the first Thursday of every month, and attendance is surprisingly good considering it's over lunchtime.
Interviewer: Could I ask you to speak up a little? The recorder is across the table.
Chief Compliance Officer: Certainly. I tend to trail off at the end of sentences, so do stop me if I become hard to hear on the recording.
Interviewer: I'll try not to keep you much longer than planned.
Chief Compliance Officer: No rush from my side. I'd much rather we cover things properly than cut the conversation short because of the clock.
Interviewer: How do you find the printers?
Chief Compliance Officer: Dreadful. They jam constantly, and nobody ever replaces the paper, so I've more or less stopped printing anything at all.
Interviewer: What do you think of the Monday all-staff emails?
Chief Compliance Officer: A bit much, honestly. They're far too long and I tend to skim them over a coffee and forget everything by lunchtime.
Interviewer: Do you have a favourite part of the building?
Chief Compliance Officer: The old library on the second floor. They kept the shelves when the offices were redone, and it's the quietest room we have, so it's always the first to be booked.
Interviewer: What do people do for lunch?
Chief Compliance Officer: A mix of the canteen and the small cafe across the road. The cafe does a very good soup, and some people have their own table there on Fridays.
Interviewer: Sorry, the call dropped on my end for a second there.
Chief Compliance Officer: It was fine here, nothing missed. If it does drop again just give me a moment and I'll wait until you're back.

Plant Manager: Go ahead. I'm happy to follow wherever you want to take it, so just steer the conversation as you see fit.

Interviewer: I'll try not to keep you much longer than planned.
Plant Manager: No rush from my side. I'd much rather we cover things properly than cut the conversation short because of the clock.

Plant Manager: That sounds good to me. I tend to answer more naturally when it feels like a conversation rather than a formal interview.

Plant Manager: Take your time. I'm in no rush, and I've blocked out the whole morning for this anyway.
Interviewer: Is this still a good time, or are you expecting a call?
Plant Manager: It's fine, I've put my phone on silent. If anything urgent comes up my assistant knows where to find me.
Interviewer: What do you think of the Monday all-staff emails?
Plant Manager: A bit much, honestly. They're far too long and I tend to skim them over a coffee and forget everything by lunchtime.
Interviewer: Do you have any teams based elsewhere?
Plant Manager: A small team in Lisbon handles our invoicing. I've only met them twice, but they sent a lovely card when we hit one of our anniversaries last year.
Interviewer: What was the company like when you joined?

Plant Manager: Certainly. I tend to trail off at the end of sentences, so do stop me if I become hard to hear on the recording.
Interviewer: Did you have any trouble finding the room this morning?
Plant Manager: None at all. The reception staff pointed me over, and the signs were pretty clear once I was on the right floor.
Interviewer: Can I get you some water or a coffee before we continue?
Plant Manager: A coffee would be great, thank you. Just milk, no sugar, and there's no hurry at all.
Interviewer: How long have you been with the company?
Plant Manager: Just over nine years now. I started in a different role and moved across when the department was reorganised, which seems like a very long time ago.
Interviewer: Would you like me to send you a summary of what we discussed afterwards?
Plant Manager: That would be good, yes. Just send it to my work address, and I'll look it over when I have a quiet moment.
Interviewer: Has the office changed much recently?
Plant Manager: We moved floors a couple of years ago to make room for a new team. The new layout is brighter, though the meeting rooms are still in short supply on Tuesdays.
Interviewer: Before we go on, are you happy for me to keep recording?
Plant Manager: Yes, that's fine, go ahead. I've done a few of these before, so I know roughly how it goes.
Interviewer: Thanks, that's really helpful to hear.
Plant Manager: Happy to help. Let me know if any of it needs more detail, and I can think about it and get back to you.

Interviewer: Could you spell that name for my notes, please?

Interviewer: How are the facilities?

Interviewer: It's raining quite hard outside now, isn't it?

Interviewer: Let me know if I start running over the time we agreed.
Plant Manager: We have until the top of the hour, so we're fine. After that I do have another commitment, but it's a short walk.
Interviewer: Any thoughts on the new lanyards?
Plant Manager: Pointless, if you ask me. They keep getting caught on chairs, and I can't see who they were meant to help.
Interviewer: Where does the line lose time?
Plant Manager: Changeovers. We switch product variants about eleven times a week and each one takes around ninety minutes.
Interviewer: Is that a technical limit?
Plant Manager: No. Our best shift does it in forty minutes. The difference is that they pre-stage tooling during the previous run, and the other shifts never adopted it.
Interviewer: Why not?
Plant Manager: The practice was never written down. It lives in one shift leader's head, and he's retiring next spring.
Interviewer: What about maintenance?
Plant Manager: Mostly reactive. We only had three planned stops last quarter, and all three overran.
Interviewer: I know it's a busy week, so I really appreciate you making the time.
Plant Manager: No problem at all. I moved a meeting to make room, and honestly it's a nice break from my desk.
Interviewer: Does the company run any training programmes?
Plant Manager: There's an induction week for new starters with a tour of all the sites. It's popular, although I think people mainly enjoy the free lunch on the last day.
Interviewer: Does the company do much outside the core business?
Plant Manager: We sponsor a local charity run every autumn. About forty colleagues take part, and it's become a bit of a tradition, with a small prize for the best fancy dress.
Interviewer: What's the culture like day to day?
Plant Manager: Friendly, I'd say. We have a lunch-and-learn series on the first Thursday of every month, and attendance is surprisingly good considering it's over lunchtime.
Interviewer: Do you mind if I ask a couple of background questions first?
Plant Manager: Not at all, ask whatever you need. I'd rather you had the full picture than guessed at the parts I left out.
Interviewer: Is the heating always this warm in here?
Plant Manager: Pretty much, yes. It's a running joke in the building, and half the people on this floor keep a small fan at their desk.
Interviewer: Sorry, could you repeat that last part? I missed the end of it.
Plant Manager: Of course. It was a long answer, so don't worry if it rambled a little, I do that sometimes.
Interviewer: Does the company have a sustainability policy?
Plant Manager: We have a modest one. There's a recycling scheme on each floor, and last year we switched to a green electricity supplier, which was announced at an all-hands meeting.
Interviewer: Has the company changed its branding recently?
Plant Manager: We refreshed the logo two summers ago. It was a modest change, mostly the colours, and the printed stationery took longer to get replaced than anyone expected.
Interviewer: What do you make of the coffee here?
Plant Manager: Terrible, if I'm honest. It's the thing I complain about most, and I've started bringing my own flask in.
Interviewer: How do you find the new office layout?
Plant Manager: Honestly, a bit grim. The lighting on the fourth floor gives me a headache and I think most people would say the same if you asked them.
Interviewer: How is the IT equipment generally?
Plant Manager: Laptops get replaced every four years or so. The latest batch arrived in the autumn and people were pleased with the screens, though the chargers are a different story.
Interviewer: Do you have a favourite part of the building?
